definition: Memory is the faculty by which past experience is retained and recovered, and in PKD's work it is the fragile foundation on which personal identity rests. His recurring premise is that memory is neither reliable nor securely one's own — it can be erased, implanted, falsified, or belong to someone else — so that the continuity of the self it is supposed to guarantee becomes radically uncertain.
pkd_relevance: If identity is what you remember, and memory can be manufactured, then the self is hostage to whoever controls the record. PKD grasped this early and returned to it obsessively, using memory manipulation as the lever that pries open his characters' worlds. Memory also connects his psychological concerns to his metaphysical ones: false memory in the fiction anticipates the recovered 'true' memory of anamnesis in the Exegesis.
in_the_fiction: We Can Remember It for You Wholesale sells implanted vacation memories and then cannot tell the real from the fake, leaving Quail unsure which of his lives actually happened. Ubik makes memory and perception decay in real time. Do Androids Dream and Blade Runner turn on implanted memories that make androids feel human, and across the corpus characters routinely discover that what they remember was installed or edited.
in_the_exegesis: Memory shifts register in the Exegesis, where PKD reframes it through Platonic anamnesis — 'un-forgetting' — as the recovery of knowledge from a prior or truer existence. The unreliable, manipulable memory of the fiction becomes, in his 2-3-74 theorizing, a channel through which suppressed reality can break back in. PKD develops this at length, connecting ordinary memory, false memory, and salvific recollection into a single spectrum.
intellectual_background: The philosophical background runs from Locke's memory theory of personal identity through Plato's doctrine of recollection to Bergson and Proust on memory and duration. PKD also drew on contemporary anxieties about brainwashing, hypnosis, and behavioral conditioning, and on his reading in the psychology of false and repressed memory, which he blended with the metaphysical tradition.
scholarly_debate: Critics debate whether PKD's treatment of memory is best read as epistemological skepticism (we can never verify our pasts), as a theory of the constructed self, or as covertly religious (memory as the residue of a lost divine origin). There is also discussion of how presciently he anticipated later neuroscience and legal controversies over false and implanted memory, and of whether his fiction offers any criterion for distinguishing true recollection from confabulation.
